speaker: John Carmack
title: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets (#309)
question: In interactive software engineering, how does the relationship between execution efficiency and user value determine when deep performance optimization actually pays off?
guest: So much of my systems analysis goes around understanding what the speed of light is—what would be the best you could possibly do here. And it sounds horrible, but in a lot of cases you can be 1,000 times off your speed of light velocity and it's still okay, and can even be optimal from a larger system standpoint. You don't want to parachute in someone to make a webpage run 1,000 times faster and start up in 37 milliseconds when someone right out of a boot camp can spin up an application for it; often efficiency is not really the best metric. Still, it's always good to know what you could do if you took it far, because sometimes there are discontinuities. Around user reaction times, the difference between operating in one second and 750 milliseconds is not that huge. But if you get down to 50 milliseconds, all of a sudden it feels amazing—like doing your bidding instantly rather than giving a command and waiting. So sometimes it's important to crunch hard to cross a threshold, but there are broad basins in the value metric where it just doesn't pay to go that extra mile.

points.core: Running orders of magnitude below hardware limits is often globally optimal for development.
points.note: Accept: being 100x–1,000x slower than theoretical hardware maximum is frequently optimal when it saves expensive engineering talent, speeds shipping, or improves portability. Do not credit: generic "premature optimization is bad" slogans without the larger system or resource trade-off.

points.core: User value stays nearly flat across broad intermediate latency ranges despite optimization effort.
points.note: Accept: modest speedups in slow ranges (e.g., 1 second down to 750ms) yield minimal usability gains, creating wide basins where extra optimization does not pay off. Do not credit: vague claims that users do not care about speed.

points.core: Deep optimization pays off primarily when crossing sharp perceptual thresholds like instantaneous response.
points.note: Accept: non-linear discontinuities in human reaction time (e.g., dropping latency to ~50ms or under ~100ms) where software suddenly feels instant rather than waiting on a command. Do not credit: generic statements that faster software always delights users.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Deep optimization pays off only when faster execution changes what the user experiences or can do, and that relationship is nonlinear, governed by perceptual and workflow thresholds rather than raw speed.

Human perception sets the breakpoints: roughly 100 ms feels instantaneous, about 1 second preserves flow of thought, and beyond about 10 seconds attention drifts. Shaving time within a band (say 40 ms to 20 ms, or 6 s to 5 s) yields little value, while crossing a band (3 s to 300 ms) can transform the interaction, enabling tighter iteration, exploration, and new usage patterns. Variance matters too: tail latency and jank often hurt more than a slightly slower average.

Amdahl's law applies to the human loop as well. If the user's own thinking, typing, or a network round trip dominates the cycle, speeding up the computation barely moves end-to-end time. So optimize the measured bottleneck on a frequent, user-facing path.

Deep optimization is therefore justified when it crosses a perceptual threshold, removes the dominant bottleneck in a frequently repeated loop, or cuts cost materially at scale. Otherwise, the effort and added complexity are better spent on correctness, features, or perceived responsiveness.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
In interactive software, the relationship between execution efficiency and user value is non-linear and bounded by human perception. Users experience performance through cognitive thresholds rather than raw clock cycles: responses under roughly 16 milliseconds sustain fluid animation, under 100 milliseconds feel instantaneous, and under one second preserve uninterrupted thought. Once an interaction operates comfortably beneath its perceptual ceiling, shaving off additional microseconds yields virtually zero noticeable user value.

Deep optimization therefore pays off primarily when it crosses one of these perceptual cliffs or unlocks qualitatively new workflows—such as direct manipulation or instant search-as-you-type—that slower execution makes impossible. It also pays off when resource efficiency tangibly improves battery life, enables lower-end devices, or curbs prohibitive infrastructure costs at scale. Because low-level tuning typically increases code complexity, fragility, and opportunity cost, optimizing paths that already feel fast actively harms users by delaying reliability improvements and useful features. Consequently, deep optimization is justified only when profiling confirms a bottleneck is visibly degrading user flow, device endurance, or operational viability.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
In interactive software, user value doesn't rise in a straight line with execution efficiency. It rises in steps. Human perception has rough thresholds. Under about 100 ms a response feels instant. Under about 1 second the user's flow of thought holds. Past about 10 seconds attention breaks and people switch tasks. Cutting 800 ms to 400 ms may go unnoticed. Cutting 150 ms to 60 ms, or 15 s to 2 s, changes how the tool feels and how people use it.

So deep optimization pays off mainly in two cases. The first is when it moves a frequent, user-facing interaction across one of those thresholds. Examples are keystroke latency, search-as-you-type, compile-and-test loops, and scrolling. Gains there compound across every use and every user, and they can enable new workflows, like fast iteration in place of batch-style waiting. The second is when it removes a bottleneck users actually feel, including tail latency and jank, not just averages.

The same work on rarely used paths, background jobs, or delays users already tolerate mostly adds complexity for little value. Amdahl's law applies here: speeding up a part that isn't the main source of the user's wait barely helps. So measure what users perceive first, then optimize where the step in value lies.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
In interactive software, execution efficiency translates into user value nonlinearly, governed largely by human perceptual thresholds and practical resource limits. Users experience responsiveness in distinct bands: keeping animations within a 16-millisecond frame budget preserves fluid motion, responding to input within roughly 100 milliseconds feels instantaneous, and finishing heavier tasks under a second maintains cognitive flow. Pushing performance across one of these boundaries—or eliminating visible stalls, battery drain, and excessive memory use on constrained devices—yields substantial user value.

Beyond those thresholds, however, efficiency hits sharp diminishing returns. Cutting a 5-millisecond operation to 1 millisecond is imperceptible to the user, yet deep optimization typically introduces complexity, fragility, and maintenance overhead while diverting engineering time from features or reliability. Deep optimization therefore pays off when profiling proves a bottleneck directly disrupts user flow, constrains core workflows on real-world data or hardware, or multiplies into significant infrastructure and energy costs at scale. Outside those hot paths, stopping at "perceptibly fast" maximizes overall user value.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Deep performance optimization pays off when execution speed limits something users value. Cutting a delay from two seconds to 200 milliseconds can make an editor feel responsive. Cutting a delay from two milliseconds to 200 microseconds may make no perceptible difference, though the savings can still matter if the operation runs often enough to affect battery life, capacity, or cost.

Measure performance in real workflows, find the bottleneck, and estimate what improving it would change for users. Once the interaction is reliably fast enough, further optimization is worth doing only if the gains justify the engineering time and maintenance burden.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Deep optimization pays off when faster execution meaningfully improves something users care about. Cutting a typing delay from 200 milliseconds to 20 can make an editor feel responsive. Cutting it from 2 milliseconds to 1 also looks impressive as a percentage, but users are unlikely to notice. That same millisecond can matter if the operation repeats a thousand times while someone waits.

Measure the whole interaction under realistic conditions, including slow cases that averages hide. Then weigh the expected benefit across users and repetitions against the engineering time, maintenance cost, and other improvements you could deliver. Once an interaction is reliably fast enough, further tuning earns its keep only if it creates value elsewhere, such as longer battery life, lower operating costs, or support for larger workloads.
